newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gears up for abortion on demand.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gears up for abortion on demand.

text.p: Abortion on demand, hailed as an "intoxicating" victory by pro-choice lobbyists, becomes a reality in South Africa from Saturday.

Up to 250 women a week are expected to flood the country's largest hospital, Baragwanath in the sprawling Soweto township, and authorities nationwide say they are gearing up for a rush by women nearing or already over their 12th week of pregnancy.

"We do realise that there is going to be an initial increase in the number of requests over the first couple of months, until we reach a more stable situation," said Carol Marshall, a senior health official in Gauteng encompassing Johannesburg and Soweto.
"As a ballpark figure, we expect anything from 200 to 520 (abortions) a year for every 1,000 live births."

South Africa's first democratic parliament -- in its most controversial moral question yet -- gave final approval to the liberal abortion legislation in November last year, but health authorities were given until February 1 to introduce it.

Under the new law, women and girls are entitled to a state funded abortion on demand during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy if they have no private medical aid schemes, and, subject to widely defined conditions, for a further eight weeks.
Despite strong protests from anti-abortion groups, the law specifically gives girls of any age the sole right to decide whether to have an abortion.

Helen Rees, a consultant to the national health department, told a news conference many women already in their 12th to 20th weeks of pregnancy -- who had waited for the law to come into effect -- were expected to arrive at hospitals for abortions.

"To begin with, we do anticipate that we are going to see large numbers of women in the second part of their pregnancies. That is a concern, (but) it is almost inevitable when you start a service like this," she said.

Until now, close to 50,000 women reported to hospitals each year after backstreet abortions at a cost to the state of 18.5 million rand ($4 million), and over 425 women a year died from botched abortions, medical records show.
Rees said South African health workers were optimistic the law would finally begin to put illegal abortionists out of work.

"What we're hoping is that over a period of time there will be a diminishing number of women being admitted with incomplete abortions, and a decrease in the number of women who are being admitted who are ill...I'm sure it will."
Judi Fortuin of the non-governmental National Progressive Primary Health Care Network told Reuters that pro-choice campaigners were elated the legislation was coming into force.
"It's an intoxicating feeling that on such a highly politicised issue, for once as women, we have the law on our side," she said.
Anti-abortionists however, who have maintained a vociferous campaign against abortions becoming legal, say they are planning to hold placard protests across the country from next week.
"Government must expect more and more protests," Pro-Life president Claude Newbury said. "We will continue with our campaign to defend and uphold the sanctity of life.

"One doesn't want to target women seeking abortions but to put full responsibility on the state and the medical profession which has become the most skilfull assassination force the country has seen -- real hitmen."
